content.title: Arvada Parks Turf Conversion Program
content.summary: In spring 2024, the City of Arvada Parks Department initiated a pilot turf conversion project, transitioning approximately 2.5 acres of bluegrass to native grass at two locations, later expanding to 3.5 acres at Tennyson Knolls Park in 2025. This initiative aims to conserve water, saving over 830,000 gallons annually, while also enhancing biodiversity and reducing maintenance needs. Community support for further turf conversions is strong, with 63% of residents favoring the initiative according to the 2024 Community Survey.
content.body:
![park maintenance worker driving a tractor to lay down native grass seed](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=3498 "park maintenance worker driving a tractor to lay down native grass seed")

In the spring of 2024, the City of Arvada Parks Department launched a pilot turf conversion project at two locations in the city totaling approximately 2.5 acres. In 2025, the City expanded the program to include approximately 3.5 acres at Tennyson Knolls Park.

The turf conversion pilot project is part of the [City’s commitment to water conservation](/1011) and sustainability. Once fully established, converting these areas from bluegrass to native grass will save more than **830,000****gallons of water** **and****37 hours of mowing per year.**

Learn more about each turf conversion location – [Tomlinson Park](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=6311), [Club Crest Park North](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=3711) and [Tennyson Knolls Park](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=6311) – further down this page.

## Benefits of native grass

- Once the native grass is established, there are several benefits beyond water conservation:
- Native grasses help support a balanced ecosystem by increasing biodiversity.
- Native grasses provide a habitat for pollinators (bees, butterflies, birds, bats and other animals), which provide vital but often unnoticed services.
- Healthy native grasslands filter pollutants from stormwater run-off.
- When allowed to grow to a natural height, native grasses reduce non-native weed growth.
- There are reduced chemical impacts on our environment due to the elimination of fertilizer use and fewer weeds.
- Reduced fuel emissions since the area will not be mowed regularly once the native grass is established.

The City will use this pilot project as a test case to evaluate other potential areas in the City for turf conversion.

## Community Feedback

**A majority of Arvada residents (63%) support additional conversion of turf grass to native grasses in Arvada parks.** That data is from the [City's 2024 Community Survey](https://www.arvadaco.gov/238/Community-Survey).

![bar graph showing 62.8% of residents support the additional conversion of turf grass to native grass](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6214)

1. [Tomlinson Park Turf Conversion](#tab9bca09c8-ac04-4016-9028-a1c2a9c097f5_0)

### map of Tomlinson park with a highlighted area that is labeled Turf Conversion Area

### Why this location?

One acre on the south end of [Jack B. Tomlinson Park](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SFunC4WpLEhPXbPz5) is being converted from Kentucky bluegrass to native grass. This area of Tomlinson Park was specifically chosen for several reasons:

- There are no trees, so eventually when irrigation in this area is shut off, it won’t cause any trees to die
- The area was identified as extremely low-use, meaning it’s almost never used for active or passive recreation, so the park user experience should not change
- The grass in this area was already struggling due to poor soil conditions and previous issues with water pumps used for irrigation

### Timeline

- **March of 2024**: Conversion area seeded with a native grass seed mix
- Fall of 2024: Conversion area seeded again with a native grass seed mix
- 2025 to 2029: Native grass establishment period
- Once established, the area will be maintained like our open space, meaning it will not be irrigated and will only be mowed once a year in the fall

### What Park Users Can Expect

Because this section of the park was identified as a low-use area, it’s anticipated there will be little to no effect on park users.

- We will continue to mow along both sides of the walk when needed as we have done in years past.
- There will be no changes to the grass area on the west end of the park near the playground; that area will remain bluegrass and will be maintained as usual, including aeration and overseeding in the spring and regular irrigation and mowing during the spring and summer.
- Improved water quality in the park lake.

1. [Club Crest North Turf Conversion](#tab9bca09c8-ac04-4016-9028-a1c2a9c097f5_1)

![satellite map showing an acre-sized turf conversion project  ](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=3711)

### Why this location?

The [area along the Heritage Canal Trail from Carr Drive heading west](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6cV3wP5dxzehpAG99) connecting to Club Crest Park North was chosen to be converted from bluegrass to native grass for several reasons:

- The area was identified as extremely low-use, meaning it's almost never used for active or passive recreation, so the park user experience should not change
- The topography of the area makes mowing inefficient

### Timeline

- **Spring/Summer 2024**: Irrigation in the area will be adjusted. Trees in the area will continue to be watered but the grass will be watered and mowed less frequently.
- Fall 2024: Conversion area seeded with native grass seed mix.
- 2025 to 2029: Native grass establishment period
- Once established, the area will be maintained like our open space, meaning it will not be irrigated and will only be mowed once a year in the fall

### What Park and Trail Users Can Expect

Because this section of the park was identified as a low-use area, it’s anticipated there will be little to no effect on park users, other than aesthetics.

1. [Tennyson Knolls Turf COnversion](#tab9bca09c8-ac04-4016-9028-a1c2a9c097f5_2)

[**Visit the Tennyson Knolls Park Turf Conversion Page for more information**](/1442)

![Aerial view of Tennyson Knolls Park, with 3.5 acres of the eastern side of the park highlighted ](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6311)

### Why this location?

A large section on the east side of Tennyson Knolls Park is being converted from bluegrass to native grass. This location was chosen for several reasons:

- Tennyson Knolls is a large neighborhood park that has nearly 11 acres of irrigated bluegrass; after converting 3.5 acres to native grass, there is still more than 7 acres of irrigated bluegrass in the park.
- The park’s irrigation system is outdated, with poor coverage and an inefficient design, making it difficult to keep the grass green.
- The soil quality is also poor, made up of clay and rock, which adds to the challenge of maintaining healthy turf.
- Once established, the native grass will significantly reduce costs for mowing, watering, and fertilizer.

### What Park Users Can Expect

- In some areas, you may notice dark brown plant material. This is not dead grass — it’s dead bindweed that was recently sprayed.
- The majority of irrigated bluegrass in the park (more than 7 acres) will remain and be maintained as usual.
- Over time, the converted area will transition to a natural, open-space look while still providing green space in other parts of the park.
- Trees that surround the native conversion area will still be watered regularly and are not expected to be impacted.
- The existing native grass area on the far east end of the park that connects the park to Tennyson Street will remain unchanged.
- Benefits of native grass include:
  - Less use of pesticides, fertilizers and water
  - Fewer emissions and noise pollution due to less mowing
  - A more environmentally friendly park that is a more diverse habitat for wildlife and pollinators.
